n: This lecture is devoted to methods of isolating poisonous substances from a biological specimen and purifying them, that is, extraction. Plan: the influence of the nature of the organic solvent and of pH on extraction, the influence of electrolytes, and methods of purifying isolates from foreign substances. Key terms: extraction, organic solvent, pH conditions, electrolyte, extractive substances, number of extractions, polar solvent. The isolation of poisonous substances from a biological specimen and biological fluids is carried out mainly with acidified water, alcohol or organic solvents.

Let us define the place of extraction. Extraction is one of the main methods used to isolate toxicologically significant substances from a specimen and to purify them. The transfer of a substance from one solvent to another is related to its solubility in each solvent. Distribution continues until the concentration of the substance is equalised in both solvents. At the same time, the insolubility of foreign substances, that is, protein, fat and pigments, in the solvent used for the isolation is of great importance.

We list the factors affecting extraction. The complete transfer of a substance from the aqueous solution into the organic layer is affected by the distribution coefficient and the degree of extraction. Also acting are the pH conditions, the nature of the organic solvent, the number of extractions, salting-out agents, that is, electrolytes, and temperature. The solubility of a substance is strongly affected by the nature of the solvent, the pH of the medium and electrolytes.

On the distribution coefficient K. A substance passes into the organic solvent layer depending on the distribution coefficient K: K = Corg / Csuv. Here Corg is the concentration of the substance dissolved in the organic solvent, and Csuv is the concentration of the substance dissolved in water. The conclusion: the larger K is, the more of the substance passes into the organic solvent layer.

Now, the degree of extraction R. It is expressed as a percentage: R = A / N · 100 %. Here A is the amount of substance extracted into the organic solvent, and N is the initial, that is, the total amount of the substance in the water. Remember: the larger K and R are, the more of the substance passes into the organic solvent layer.

We compare K and R. K = Corg / Csuv is the ratio of the concentrations of the substance in the organic and aqueous layers. R = A / N · 100 % is the percentage of the amount transferred into the organic solvent relative to the initial total amount. That is, K expresses a ratio of concentrations, and R a percentage of the amount. The larger K and R are, the more of the substance passes into the organic solvent layer.

t: Condition for K greater than one
n: On the condition that K be greater than one. In the saponification method, it is necessary that the distribution coefficient of the substance dissolved in the organic solvent be greater than one. For the substance dissolved in water, it must be less than one. Saponification is used for compounds resistant to hydrolysis. After hydrolysis, the main substance is extracted.

Now, the effect of pH on organic acids. Aqueous solutions of non-dissociating organic acids such as barbiturates are electrically neutral and are poorly hydrated by water molecules. When such molecules are mixed with an organic solvent, they are quickly solvated and pass into the organic layer. An acid dissociated in aqueous solution, on the other hand, is quickly hydrated by water dipoles. Because of stable hydrate bonds, it is poorly extracted.

The result of a change in pH for acids. If the medium shifts towards the alkaline side, the dissociation of the acid increases, undissociated molecules decrease, and extraction falls. If the hydrogen ion concentration shifts towards the acid side, the number of undissociated molecules increases, and extraction increases. Under such conditions even weak organic acids are in a not fully dissociated state and are extracted in large amounts.

t: Effect of pH: alkaloids and bases
n: For alkaloids and bases the effect of pH is the reverse. Alkaloids and synthetic nitrogen-containing compounds, in a neutral medium, when acid is added, form dissociating ions. Undissociated organic bases are quickly solvated and pass into the organic solvent layer. Organic bases are weak electrolytes. Therefore, if dissociation increases, extraction falls, whereas if alkali is added, extraction rises.

Amphoteric compounds. Morphine, apomorphine and salsoline, which contain an amino group and a phenol group, and ecgonine and amino acids, which contain an amino group and a carboxyl group, are amphoteric compounds. Depending on the pH of the medium, they show basic properties in an acid medium and acidic properties in an alkaline medium. Amphoteric compounds in the molecular state are readily extracted from aqueous solution with organic solvents.

Amphoteric compounds and the isoelectric point. The ions of amphoteric compounds are easily hydrated by water molecules and are practically not extracted with organic solvents. At the isoelectric point they carry no electric charge, and their reactivity falls. Proteins usually precipitate under such conditions. That is, to extract amphoteric compounds, they must be kept in the molecular, uncharged state.

General conclusion on pH. Barbiturates and compounds with acidic properties are well extracted in an acid medium. Alkaloids do not pass into the organic layer in an acid medium and remain in the aqueous solution. To isolate them, alkali is added to convert them to the base form, and they are extracted. The table gives the groups of substances and the medium suited to them, while neutral substances are extracted in any medium.

t: pH and ionisation: acids and bases
n: We compare acids and bases with respect to pH and ionisation. Substances with acidic properties, for example barbiturates, do not dissociate in an acid medium and are well extracted. Alkaloids and nitrogen-containing synthetic bases are ionised in an acid medium and remain in water; after alkali is added and they are converted to the base form, they are extracted. For neutral substances such as antifebrin and phenacetin, pH has little effect.

Neutral substances. For neutral substances such as antifebrin and phenacetin, the effect of pH is small. They are well extracted by organic solvents in acid, neutral and alkaline media. In the isolate obtained in an acid medium, barbiturates, neutral substances, for example phenacetin, and organic acids, that is, salicylic and picric acid, are examined.

The nature of the organic solvent. The character of the organic solvents also has a great effect on the degree of extraction. For a more complete isolation of poisonous, narcotic and intoxicating substances, their solubility in organic solvents is taken into account. According to the qualification material, the yield of phenobarbital and hexamidine differs between chloroform and diethyl ether. The tables are given later in this topic.

The number of extractions. In isolating most poisonous, narcotic and intoxicating substances from the aqueous layer, the number of extractions has an effect. The number of extractions is found empirically. In the experiment from the qualification, 4 and 5 extractions did not appreciably increase the amount of phenobarbital and hexamidine. Therefore 3 extractions with chloroform are sufficient.

t: Phenobarbital: solvent and number of extractions
n: The effect of solvent and number of extractions for phenobarbital. With chloroform, 10 ml each time, the yield is 74.54 % the 1st time, 88.35 % the 2nd, 92.83 % the 3rd, 93.30 % the 5th. With diethyl ether, 10 ml each time: 91.31 % the 1st time, 93.62 % the 2nd, 95.32 % the 3rd, 96.02 % the 5th. So for phenobarbital, diethyl ether gave a higher yield than chloroform.

t: Hexamidine: solvent and number of extractions
n: For hexamidine the result is different. With chloroform, 10 ml each time, the yield is 79.33 % the 1st time, 89.31 % the 2nd, 91.84 % the 3rd, 92.31 % the 5th. With diethyl ether, hexamidine passes poorly: 14.92 % the 1st time, 24.45 % the 3rd, 27.67 % the 5th. So for hexamidine, chloroform is considerably more effective than diethyl ether.

The effect of electrolytes and salting out. If an electrolyte is added to a solution of an organic compound readily soluble in water, the solubility changes: it may increase or decrease. A decrease in solubility is called an increase in salting out, and an increase in solubility a decrease in salting out. As a result of salting out, extraction with an organic solvent increases, that is, the distribution coefficient increases.

The salting-out effect of electrolytes depends on the nature of the substance being salted out and of the salting-out agent, on its concentration and on the ionic radius. The salting-out effect of ions with a small radius is greater than that of ions with a large radius. An electrolyte is also used in breaking emulsions and precipitating protein substances. In some cases, under the influence of an electrolyte, the degree of recovery of a substance from the aqueous solution falls appreciably.

The effect of temperature. With a change in temperature, the extraction of substances may increase or decrease. This depends on the change of the distribution coefficient under the influence of temperature. With a change in temperature, the stages of dissociation and association, hydration and solvation in the phases also change.

t: Purifying isolates: why it is needed
n: Now we consider why purification of isolates is needed. After isolation with polar solvents, residues of two kinds of isolate, obtained in acid and alkaline media, are formed. In them, together with the isolated substance, there are co-extracted foreign substances such as proteins, amino acids, fat and lipids. Foreign substances interfere with the analysis, and sometimes give a product with reagents like that of the substance under examination. They also have a negative effect on quantitative analysis.

Purification methods: straining and filtration. The main purification methods are straining, filtration, centrifugation, precipitation and re-extraction. Straining is done through cotton wool or bandage and removes large mechanical impurities. However, cotton wool adsorbs the substance to be determined, which causes losses. Filtration removes large and small mechanical impurities, but filter paper also adsorbs the substance. For this reason centrifugation is considered more convenient.

Centrifugation and precipitation. Centrifugation purifies the isolate of large and small mechanical impurities with the help of centrifuges. Proteins and polypeptides are precipitated with trichloroacetic, tungstic and metaphosphoric acids and some heteropoly compounds. By heating the solution to about 40 °C, much protein can be precipitated. Absolute ethyl and methyl alcohol or acetone also precipitate protein. In the salting-out method, proteins precipitate in a saturated salt solution.

Repeated extraction, that is, re-extraction: the acid isolate. Organic acids and barbiturates are purified by extraction and re-extraction. First alkali is added to the residue, pH 13: here the organic layer is not needed, the alkaline aqueous layer is. Then the aqueous layer is acidified, pH 1, and re-extracted. Now the required substance is in the organic layer.

Re-extraction: the alkaline isolate. Alkaloids and their synthetic analogues are also purified by re-extraction. Here the order is reversed. Acid is added to the residue, pH 1: the organic layer is not needed, the acid aqueous layer is. The aqueous layer is made alkaline, pH 13, and re-extracted. As a result the required substance is in the organic layer.

Conditions and limitations of re-extraction. In purification by re-extraction, the pH of the medium must be exact. If this is not attended to, the substance under examination may be lost. In the acid scheme, neutral substances and substances with weak base properties cannot be purified, because they are lost during purification. In the alkaline scheme, substances with weak base properties are lost, that is, purine derivatives, narcotine, promedol, antipyrine and amidopyrines.

Saponification. Saponification is used for compounds resistant to hydrolysis. For example, in purifying organochlorine compounds from fat, the fat is hydrolysed. After hydrolysis, the main substance is extracted.

Sulphonation is used in purifying extracts rich in fat and lipids. It makes it possible to isolate substances resistant to concentrated sulphuric acid, for example barbiturates. In purifying isolated substances, saponification, re-extraction, sulphonation, chromatography and fat precipitation are used.

Precipitating fat and waxy substances. The method is based on the reduced solubility of fat and waxy substances in the cold in solvents such as acetone and acetonitrile. When an acetone solution is cooled to −70 °C, the dissolved fat and waxy substances float up and separate. The precipitation of fat and waxy substances is given as one of the methods of purifying isolated substances.

Dry distillation, that is, sublimation. Dry distillation is used in purifying substances that sublime under the action of heat. Such substances include barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids, and caffeine. Other purification methods are carried out together with the isolation methods: filtration, precipitation of proteins with alcohol or an electrolyte, and centrifugation.

We summarise the physicochemical purification methods. Dry distillation is used for sublimable substances: barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids, caffeine. Electrodialysis is used in isolating and purifying substances such as strychnine and pachycarpine. In chromatographic purification, thin-layer, gel column and paper chromatography are used most. The table gives the method, the substances for which it is used, and its principle.

Electrodialysis and electrophoresis. Electrodialysis is used in isolating and purifying certain substances such as strychnine and pachycarpine. Alkaloid salts move under a direct current through a semipermeable membrane to the cathode, and for analysis the cathode liquid is extracted. Electrophoresis is chromatographic purification under the action of an electric current. In it, salts with basic properties move towards the cathode at different speeds and are separated from each other and from foreign substances.

Chromatographic purification. The most used methods are thin-layer chromatography, gel column chromatography and paper chromatography. In these methods, besides purification, the identity of the substance under examination is also determined. Different mobile systems, sorbents and detecting reagents are used. For barbiturates: chloroform - n-butanol - 25% NH4OH, ratio 70:40:5, detecting reagent, mercury sulphate and 0.02% diphenylcarbazone, spots ink-coloured, Rf values differing. For alkaloids: chloroform - acetone - diethylamine 50:30:2 or chloroform - acetone - ammonia 30:20:2, detecting reagent, Dragendorff reagent.

Purification by gel chromatography. In Kramarenko's method, the acid aqueous extract, after centrifugation, is purified of foreign substances by gel chromatography. The sorbent is Sephadex of grades G-25 and G-50. High-molecular-weight foreign organic substances pass through without being absorbed into the Sephadex pores. Barbiturates, however, are absorbed into the pores and remain in the Sephadex. The Sephadex is washed with sulphuric acid, the eluent is extracted with chloroform, and the barbiturates are examined.

Two chloroform isolates. Whatever method is used, two chloroform solutions isolated from the biomaterial are examined. The first contains substances isolated from the aqueous solution with an organic solvent in an acid medium. The second contains substances that pass into the organic layer in an alkaline medium. Each isolate is analysed separately.

We conclude the lecture. Extraction is affected by K and R, pH, the nature of the solvent, the number of extractions, electrolytes and temperature. Acidic substances are extracted in an acid medium and basic substances in an alkaline medium, while neutral substances are little affected by pH. Purification from foreign substances: straining, filtration, centrifugation, precipitation, re-extraction and physicochemical methods, that is, sublimation, electrodialysis and chromatography. For self-check, define K and R and draw the re-extraction scheme with pH values.
